meta_story.title: Liberty and Its Limits
meta_story.tagline: Six lives inside a contested revolution
meta_story.description: American revolutionaries fought an empire with armies, pamphlets, diplomatic missions, household labor, political argument, and financial improvisation. George Washington and Alexander Hamilton helped turn resistance into military victory and then into a functioning national government; Benjamin Franklin secured essential French support and helped frame the constitutional settlement. Their achievements depended as well on voices often kept beyond formal power, including Abigail Adams and Phillis Wheatley, who made the Revolution’s claims answerable to women, enslaved people, families, and public opinion.

hints.hint: Focus on the struggle for independence and the contested work of building the early United States; balance military command, diplomacy, political advocacy, correspondence, constitutional design, and public finance.

chapters.title: Crisis in Word and Arms (1773-1775)

person_events.theme_connection: Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral was Wheatley's landmark published collection, making an enslaved African woman's intellectual authority visible across the Atlantic. Its durable literary and public intervention made Revolutionary-era ideals of liberty and equality answerable to Black people excluded from formal political power.

Washington’s appointment and assumption of command created the unified Continental Army leadership necessary to turn colonial resistance into an organized war for independence. His command became the central military institution of the Revolution.

Wheatley’s poem “To His Excellency, George Washington,” subsequently circulated in print, gave the Patriot cause a powerful Black woman’s literary voice. Its address to the commander in chief made revolutionary ideals and public patriotism answerable to an enslaved African-born poet.

historical_context.title: Intolerable Acts
historical_context.description: Parliament's punitive measures against Massachusetts helped draw George Washington into intercolonial resistance as a Virginia delegate to the First Continental Congress.

chapters.lead_in: As resistance hardened into war, Wheatley claimed public authority through poetry and Washington assumed command of a continental army. Revolutionary action began in both language and force.

chapters.title: War and Revolutionary Claims (1776-1781)

person_events.theme_connection: In her “Remember the Ladies” letter, Adams made women’s political status an explicit challenge to the new republic’s lawmaking. This enduring intervention is a landmark articulation of the gap between revolutionary liberty and women’s exclusion from formal power.

Franklin’s diplomacy helped secure French material support and the 1778 alliance, without which American independence was far less attainable; he also helped negotiate the 1783 peace. These agreements were lasting diplomatic instruments that transformed the war into an international struggle and secured U.S. independence.

Washington’s victories at Trenton and Princeton revived the Continental cause after its retreat through New Jersey, preserving morale, enlistments, and confidence in the army. They were pivotal battlefield achievements in the path to independence.

Hamilton’s leadership of the assault on Redoubt No. 10 was a decisive action in the Yorktown siege, helping seal the encirclement that compelled Cornwallis’s surrender. It is a landmark example of the military path by which independence was won.

Washington’s command at Yorktown delivered the war’s decisive victory over Cornwallis, while his later resignation of command established a powerful republican precedent of civilian supremacy over the military. Together these actions mark both independence won and the character of the new republic contested and defined.

historical_context.title: Declaration of Independence
historical_context.description: The declaration made Franklin a signatory of independence, gave Washington's army a national cause, and sharpened the revolutionary arguments in Abigail Adams's correspondence and Wheatley's poetry.

chapters.lead_in: Diplomacy and battlefield victories kept independence within reach, while Adams challenged the political exclusions embedded in revolutionary lawmaking. Yorktown brought military success and set the stage for Washington’s republican surrender of command.

chapters.title: A Constitution Takes Hold (1784-1789)

person_events.theme_connection: Brant’s leadership in establishing the Six Nations community on the Grand River created a durable Haudenosaunee political homeland after Revolutionary dispossession. It concretely demonstrates Indigenous nation-building and the contest over sovereignty and land that accompanied the new republic.

Hamilton drafted the Annapolis Convention report calling for a broader convention, the decisive procedural step that led to Philadelphia in 1787. This concrete political intervention made the replacement of the failing Confederation structure possible.

Hamilton’s arguments for an energetic national government and his central authorship of the Federalist essays supplied a lasting intellectual defense of the Constitution. The essays remain a foundational artifact of the republic’s ratification and constitutional interpretation.

person_events.event_title: Signs the New United States Constitution
person_events.theme_connection: Franklin’s support for compromise and signature helped legitimize the completed Constitution at a critical moment. His intervention embodied the settlement-making required to turn revolutionary independence into a workable constitutional republic.

As unanimously chosen presiding officer, Washington lent indispensable authority and order to the Constitutional Convention as it produced the proposed Constitution. His leadership was central to converting the failed Articles framework into a new national governing charter.

As first treasury secretary, Hamilton organized a national fiscal administration and advanced federal debt assumption and customs-based revenue. This was a foundational institutional system that made the new constitutional government financially viable and politically consequential.

Washington’s inauguration as the first president put the Constitution’s new executive branch into operation. Establishing that office under a leader who had surrendered military command was an irreplaceable milestone in creating the republic.

historical_context.title: Shays' Rebellion
historical_context.description: The uprising alarmed Washington and Hamilton and became a powerful argument for the stronger federal system they pursued at the Constitutional Convention.

chapters.lead_in: Peace opened competing projects of political reconstruction: Brant helped establish a Haudenosaunee homeland, while Hamilton, Franklin, and Washington helped replace the Confederation with a stronger federal government. The Constitution then had to become an operating state.

chapters.title: Federal Power Tested (1794-1796)

person_events.theme_connection: Washington’s mobilization against the Whiskey Rebellion established that the federal government could enforce democratically enacted law against armed domestic resistance. It was a defining early test of the Constitution’s practical authority and of the limits of republican dissent.

Washington’s widely circulated Farewell Address created a lasting statement of republican political principles, urging national unity and warning against factionalism and permanent foreign entanglements. His voluntary refusal of a third term also established a foundational republican precedent for peaceful limitation of executive power.

historical_context.title: Jay Treaty
historical_context.description: Washington's contested agreement with Britain relied on Hamilton's private advice and public defense, deepening the political divisions confronting the new administration.

chapters.lead_in: The new government asserted its authority against armed resistance as political divisions deepened around federal and foreign policy. Washington’s farewell paired warnings about faction with a voluntary relinquishment of power.

conclusion.text: By 1796, independence had been secured and the Constitution’s government had acquired leaders, finances, and the capacity to enforce its laws. Washington’s departure affirmed a peaceful limit on executive power even as his warning against faction reflected divisions already visible in the contest between Hamilton and his opponents.

Yet the nation’s institutional success did not resolve the Revolution’s deepest claims. Wheatley’s authorship, Adams’s political argument, and Brant’s work to establish a Haudenosaunee homeland all marked boundaries the formal republic had not erased. Independence created a government; it did not make liberty equal or uncontested.

circles.title: A Republic in Letters
circles.text: Franklin and Abigail Adams occupied overlapping worlds of founding politics, diplomacy, education, and correspondence. Franklin worked with John Adams and Thomas Jefferson on independence and with Adams and John Jay in Europe; Abigail made John Adams’s household a place of sustained political argument. Her father William Smith also connected her intellectual formation to the educational institutions Franklin helped establish in Philadelphia.

circles.title: Command and Contested Freedom
circles.text: Washington’s command connected him closely to Hamilton, first as an aide-de-camp and later as treasury secretary, while Wheatley addressed the general in verse and received his praise. His relationship with Brant followed a starkly different course: wartime destruction of Haudenosaunee communities was followed by a 1792 meeting over Indigenous affairs. Around Washington, military partnership, literary recognition, federal power, and contested sovereignty converged.

events.event_title: Signs the New United States Constitution

stops.title: An Atlantic Alliance
stops.text: Franklin’s 1776 mission to Paris sought the foreign support the revolutionary war required. French aid and the eventual alliance transformed a colonial rebellion into an international conflict and made American independence far more attainable.

stops.title: Victory at Yorktown
stops.text: Washington commanded the allied siege that forced Cornwallis’s surrender. Hamilton’s nighttime assault on Redoubt No. 10 tightened the encirclement, linking his ambition for battlefield command to the war’s decisive victory.

stops.title: Designing the Republic
stops.text: Philadelphia joined revolutionary command to constitutional government. Washington received command of the Continental Army there, then presided over the 1787 convention as Hamilton argued for stronger national power and Franklin urged acceptance of the completed Constitution. In 1796, Washington’s published farewell announced his retirement and warned against faction.

stops.title: Government Becomes Practice
stops.text: In New York City, Washington’s 1789 inauguration put the new executive branch into operation. His appointment of Hamilton as the first treasury secretary gave the federal government a fiscal administration and an ambitious program for national finance.

stops.title: Authority Meets Resistance
stops.text: Resistance to the federal whiskey excise made western Pennsylvania an early test of constitutional power. Washington’s mobilization of militia forces demonstrated that the new government could enforce federal law, while defining limits on armed republican dissent.

image.caption: General George Washington resigning his commission

opening.text: Between 1773 and 1796, resistance to British rule became a war, a constitutional experiment, and a functioning federal government. George Washington, Benjamin Franklin, and Alexander Hamilton helped drive that transformation through military command, diplomacy, constitutional advocacy, and public administration.

description.text: The Revolution also generated claims its institutions did not fully answer. Phillis Wheatley made an enslaved Black woman’s literary authority visible across the Atlantic, and Abigail Adams pressed the language of liberty toward women’s political standing.

image.caption: 1821 survey of Grand River Indian lands

description.text: For Joseph Brant and the Haudenosaunee, American victory brought dispossession rather than liberation. His leadership at the Grand River placed Indigenous nation-building beside the United States’ constitutional project, revealing rival claims to land and sovereignty beneath the founding of the republic.

These lives belong together because independence was never merely a battlefield result. It was a continuing contest over who could speak for liberty, who could wield national power, and whose freedom the new order would protect.

timeline.text: Parliament’s punitive measures against Massachusetts drew the colonies toward coordinated resistance. Once the Declaration of Independence gave Washington’s army a national cause, its principles also sharpened the arguments carried through Adams’s correspondence and Wheatley’s poetry.

Victory did not settle how the former colonies would govern themselves. Shays’ Rebellion strengthened demands for a more powerful federal system, while the later controversy over the Jay Treaty exposed the political divisions developing within Washington’s administration. Across these years, revolutionary mobilization became constitutional authority—and that authority faced tests of its own.

network.text: Armies, households, literary patronage, diplomatic missions, and political rivalries bound these lives into a wider founding generation. Washington occupied the densest center, but the relationships around him did not produce a single understanding of freedom: they carried admiration and collaboration alongside exclusion, rivalry, and armed conflict.

map.text: The struggle moved between an Atlantic diplomatic capital, a decisive Virginia battlefield, the political centers of Philadelphia and New York, and communities resisting federal policy in western Pennsylvania. At each place, an abstract claim became concrete: foreign support, military victory, constitutional design, executive administration, or enforcement by force.

composition.throughline: Six lives reveal the American Revolution as both a struggle for independence and an argument over what liberty would mean. Washington, Franklin, and Hamilton helped win the war and build federal power, while Wheatley, Adams, and Brant exposed exclusions involving race, gender, land, and sovereignty. Their connections show that the republic emerged through words, relationships, institutions, and force.
